stories.primary_headline: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope

primary_source.headline: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope
primary_source.content: Raye is the 35th winner of the Mercury Prize, which was established to recognise albums that push the boundaries of music A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood glamour, it beat the likes of Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean and Jade to scoop the £25,000 prize. "I couldn't tell you how grateful I am to be holding this," said Raye, clutching her trophy at Newcastle's Utilita Arena. "I'm shaking, I'm jet-lagged, I'm tired. It's all blurry." It is the first time a pop album has won the coveted prize - which recognises the best British or Irish album of the last 12 months - since M People's Elegant Slumming in 1994. Speaking to the BBC afterwards, Raye said she'd "poured everything I had" into the record, which features the global hit song Where Is My Husband? "I made this album not focusing on commercial [success], not focusing on making things cookie-cutter," said the 28-year-old.

sources.headline: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope

The 28-year-old artist, who expressed profound gratitude at Newcastle's Utilita Arena, beat nominees including Sir Paul McCartney, securing the £25,000 prize. Her victory underscores a critical shift in the Mercury Prize's recognition criteria, celebrating an album Raye described as non-commercial and deeply personal, featuring the global hit "Where Is My Husband?". stories.primary_headline: Shovel Dance Collective: Everything in Readiness review – ecstatic, dissonant folk music fighting for sonic and spiritual freedom

primary_source.headline: Shovel Dance Collective: Everything in Readiness review – ecstatic, dissonant folk music fighting for sonic and spiritual freedom
primary_source.content: (tak:til)The nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to traditional music, sounding raging, lo-fi and joyful as they link Britain’s violent past to its presentThose thus far unaware of Shovel Dance Collective’s bracing approach to folk should probably note that their third album is not much interested in breaking newcomers in gently. Everything in Readiness kicks off with a three-song suite that lasts more than 10 minutes and takes you, via a series of dramatic sonic jump-cuts, from a grinding one-note drone to a reel that seems to split the difference between trad folk fiddle-playing and the punishing squall of the Velvet Underground’s Black Angel’s Death Song. It then leaps to Tally Ho! Hark Away!, which sets a hunting song first collected in the late 1940s over a blast of what might best be described as ecstatic noise. It’s genuinely hard to work out what instruments are involved in the clattering arrhythmic chaos behind the vocal – there’s definitely a heavily distorted guitar in the mix – but the effect is weirdly euphoric rather than claustrophobic: a kind of purgative release after the mounting weirdness of the preceding reel.If you’re looking for evidence that the nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to folk music, then there it is. The glib shorthand is that they’re doing for traditional English music what Lankum have done for its Irish equivalent – joining the dots with the kind of out-there experimentation that fills the pages of the Wire magazine – although it should be pointed out they sound almost nothing like Lankum. Anyone who already has an interest in leftfield explorations of British musical history might suggest their chaotic collage approach feels more akin to the fascinating collections of field recordings, folk song and avant garde composition released by Todmorden-based label Folklore Tapes. The music on Everything in Readiness careens unpredictably from gentle lo-fi recordings caked in distortion and tape hiss to the tumultuous, surging racket they serve up on their version of the traditional coalminer’s song Jowl, Jowl and Listen; from singing unaccompanied by anything but the sound of birdsong to the disquieting ambient shimmer of Who Killed Cock Robin? A Summoning (Kind Morning in our Fists), which sounds like it was recorded in a vast, echoing crypt. Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: Loidis: From the Toolkit of Lovers review – epic 111-minute album is a teeming universe of detail

primary_source.headline: Loidis: From the Toolkit of Lovers review – epic 111-minute album is a teeming universe of detail
primary_source.content: (Incienso)Brian Leeds, AKA Huerco S, keeps raising the temperature on his once-chilly ambient on an ambitious record full of delightful detail and ASMR-inducing sound designThe sun barely seemed to rise in the earlier work of US electronic producer Brian Leeds. As Huerco S he put out the audio equivalent of 5pm November gloaming: lo-fi, low-lumen ambient and house music, flickering as if through a thicket of pine. But the light sharpened on his 2022 album Plonk, and for his project Loidis – on 2024 album One Day and this year’s stunning remix of James K’s Peel – the temperature seemed to rise along with the tempos. It wasn’t quite Balearic summer, but certainly Baltic spring or Adriatic autumn.His new album is his grandest statement across either project: 111 minutes of music across six sides of vinyl, a scale he goes a long way towards justifying. In tracks reminiscent of the microhouse sound of early 00s acts such as Luomo, the synth chords have Leeds’ trademark degraded shimmer, paired with ticklish snares and delightful ASMR-inducing sound design, stereo effects panning from right to left with quicksilver physicality. It’s hugely pleasurable to let your mind zoom in and out of these arrangements, marvelling at the microscopic detail then appreciating the overarching sense of groove, further enhanced by big melodic motifs: the playful echoing notes in TT Stunt, or the Afrobeat bassline of Running Rich. A couple of tracks in the second half lack the adventure elsewhere, but at least 90 of the minutes here are riveting, psychedelic even on nothing stronger than a cup of tea. Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: Basma and Temir Alcy: NAD review – skulking, sultry French-Moroccan crew evoke this shifting season

primary_source.headline: Basma and Temir Alcy: NAD review – skulking, sultry French-Moroccan crew evoke this shifting season
primary_source.content: (Stroom)Vocalist Basma and group Temir Alcy offer a dark and disorienting listen that contemplates loss and new beginnings, stoking a captivating sense of tensionThe new album from French-Moroccan vocalist Basma and Paris-based group Temir Alcy comes just in time for the changing of the clocks. It’s a dark and disorientating listen, exploring themes of loss and new beginnings over swampy, downtempo rhythms. The 11 tracks here linger somewhere between folk, shoegaze and ambient, with skulking percussion, droning passages and plucked strings soaked in reverb. Opening track Belati sets the tone with its spacious, shapeshifting composition, where ghostly drones and Basma’s layered calls give way to a sluggish beat. Most of the tracks follow a similar non-structure: amorphous but with an intermittent, sultry groove, like the winding bass on Khti Sarah, or the slow, swinging rhythm on Aji M3aya.Basma’s performance is always captivating. Singing in a mixture of Darija (vernacular Arabic) and French, she delivers poetic snapshots in sensory terms that chime with the shifting seasons: “shy light”, blowing wind and bonfires. On Rised, breathy fragments are looped and reversed into a dreamy haze, while her lilting chants on La Tourne have a hypnotic effect. On standout Al Atlal, which lumbers along like a haunted lullaby, she drifts between soft wails and stoic spoken word. Continue reading...

primary_source.content: England’s talent from Harrow can become the youngest female international master in chess historyBodhana Sivanandan, 11, who needed just a few rating points to qualify for an open international master title and to break Judit Polgar’s world age record, went very close to a draw against the former world title challenger GM Aleksandra Goryachkina in round one of this week’s European Club Cup, then outplayed her IM opponent in round three to take her rating to 2399.4 against the 2400 needed. In her next game, she drew from a winning position against GM Nino Batsiashvili, rated 2426.Sivanandan has thus already joined the 10 youngest 2400-rated players of all time, who include the new Russian star Roman Shogdzhiev, the world No 5, Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Argentina’s Faustino Oro, and Turkey’s Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus. brief_bullets: Sonakshi Sinha and Zaheer Iqbal star in Tu Hai Meri Kiran, a critically panned cinematic release that has faced overwhelming backlash from reviewers. Critics universally dismissed the feature as hare-brained and uninspired, noting that its convoluted narrative and weak execution provoke little more than eye-rolls from audiences. Despite the star power of its lead actors, the project has failed to resonate commercially or artistically within the competitive entertainment landscape, highlighting ongoing challenges for contemporary romantic dramas striving to capture meaningful viewer engagement and positive critical reception.
why_it_matters_bullets: Critical failures like this highlight the growing disconnect between star-driven casts and audience demand for quality scripts.

brief_bullets: The newly released cinematic feature Doosra emerges as an ambitious creative experiment that ultimately struggles to fulfill its conceptual potential. Despite exploring compelling thematic territory and attempting innovative storytelling frameworks, the production fails to sustain narrative cohesion across its runtime. sources.headline: Sunny Deol’s Suryaa: IMA seeks ban on film; CBFC says film yet to be certified

brief_bullets: The Indian Military Association has formally petitioned authorities to ban Sunny Deol’s upcoming film Suryaa, citing potential misrepresentations that could undermine the dignity of armed forces personnel. In response to the growing controversy, the Central Board of Film Certification clarified that the movie has not yet undergone official screening or certification processes. This preemptive friction highlights the intensifying scrutiny filmmakers face regarding national security narratives. As production houses navigate heightened sensitivities, the unfolding dispute underscores the delicate balance between creative expression and institutional reputation in contemporary Indian cinema.
why_it_matters_bullets: This preemptive backlash threatens to disrupt production timelines and escalate censorship debates across India's film industry.

stories.primary_headline: ‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four - or, possibly, five - of the year’s biggest films

primary_source.headline: ‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four - or, possibly, five - of the year’s biggest films
primary_source.content: New film Fatherland took Sandra Hüller back to a divided Germany. She talks about damaged dreams, Hollywood feelgood and - just maybe - appearing in the new Marvel movieSandra Hüller is crying, and it feels very strange. A wildly gifted actor, she can convey every human emotion there is. On screen, though, she is most often asked to embody deep self-possession. Even doing karaoke, Hüller is in control. And in real life, life is good. Her 2026 will end with four high-profile movies this year alone. Two (Fatherland and Rose) are black-and-white arthouse films that centre on her brilliance, and though one of the others (Digger) is already a Hollywood cautionary tale, a second (Project Hail Mary) was a giant $684m hit. (There may also be a fifth movie, bigger still. We will come back to that.)And yet, dressed in film star black, she is in tears. “This is really hard for me,” she says. Continue reading...

sources.headline: ‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four - or, possibly, five - of the year’s biggest films

brief_bullets: Acclaimed German actor Sandra Hüller reflects on a monumental career apex defined by starring roles in a remarkable slate of major international films, including arthouse projects like Fatherland and Rose, alongside blockbusters such as Project Hail Mary. Despite her extraordinary talent, established global prominence, and upcoming cinematic slate, Hüller remains notably grounded, expressing humility and emotional vulnerability regarding her rapid ascent to mainstream stardom. Her diverse portfolio bridges intimate European auteur cinema with major Hollywood productions, cementing her status as one of the most versatile and influential performers working in contemporary global film.
why_it_matters_bullets: Huller's crossover success bridges European arthouse prestige with dominant Hollywood blockbusters, redefining modern global stardom.

primary_source.headline: Sriram Raghavan at SCREEN Academy Masterclass: ‘Film logic and cinema logic are different’

sources.headline: Sriram Raghavan at SCREEN Academy Masterclass: ‘Film logic and cinema logic are different’

brief_bullets: Acclaimed filmmaker Sriram Raghavan delivered a profound masterclass at the SCREEN Academy, illuminating the fundamental creative friction between narrative film logic and the sensory demands of cinematic storytelling. During the session, the director unpacked his signature approach to crafting suspense, emphasizing that technical mechanics and character motivation must ultimately serve the visceral, immediate experience of the theatrical audience. By dissecting his acclaimed thrillers, Raghavan offered aspiring creators vital industry insights into balancing airtight plotting with cinematic atmosphere. This high-profile educational engagement underscores the academy's ongoing mission to elevate contemporary filmmaking standards through master-level mentorship from industry icons.
why_it_matters_bullets: The masterclass elevates emerging talent by translating auteur methodologies into actionable cinematic frameworks for the industry.
